# Block 4: Instructions and skills {.unnumbered} In this block you write your conventions down once, so that every conversation follows them. You use two kinds of file: an instruction fileA file the assistant loads into every conversation, such as AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, stating the project’s standing conventions. Its contents are requests, not guarantees., which loads every time, and a skillA folder containing a SKILL.md file (and optionally scripts and templates) that an assistant loads only when it is invoked by name or judged relevant from its description., which loads only when needed. Both are requests that the model usually follows; [Block 5](11f-enforced-controls.qmd) covers rules that always hold. *⏱ ~35 minutes · Start on `main`, Git pane clean, Claude Code running in Manual mode.* :::{#block4-files .callout-note collapse="true"} ## This block's files, and how it fits This block uses the same repository and data as Block 3, but nothing here depends on Block 3's scripts. Short of time? `checkpoint-skills` holds Blocks 3 and 4 finished; Block 5 starts from `main` or that branch. The optional `pub-figures` bundle is in *Going further*. | File | Where it comes from | Used in | |---|---|---| | `AGENTS.md`, `tests/test_controls.R` | Shipped: the starter instruction file, which you make yours, and a test. The test checks that the file keeps its canary and `git status` rule, Manual mode and the deny rules | Activity 1 | | `data/raw/voles_metabolism.csv` | Shipped: the data the figures show | Activity 2 | | `.agents/skills/`, `.claude/skills/` | Shipped with the course's own skills, `clean-with-codebook` and `characterisation-refactor`, for Blocks 7 and 8; you add `house-figures` to both | Activity 2, step 2 | | `scripts/fig_house.R` | The agent, using your skill | Activity 2, step 3 | | `docs/ai-log.md` | You, in Block 3; if it is missing, create it with `usethis::edit_file("docs/ai-log.md")` | Activity 2, step 5: you add a line | ::: ## Activity 1: Make AGENTS.md yours :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Edit, check, verify (12 minutes) :::: ::::{.task-container} **Goal:** make `AGENTS.md` describe your own practice and prove Claude Code loads it, so that every later conversation starts from your conventions. **Start state:** your workshop repository on `main`, Git pane clean, Claude Code running in Manual mode in the Terminal tab ([checking work](11a-setup-claude-code.qmd#checking-work)). :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Using another tool The activities use Claude Code. **Posit Assistant** reads the same `AGENTS.md`: open it from the gear menu (*Open project memory*), or describe your conventions and run `/savememory`. If the canary is missing, check that you trusted the workspace. It reads skills from `.agents/skills/` directly, so it needs no copy in `.claude/skills/`. Invoke a skill by name in the same way. For other tools, see *Instruction and skill files in other tools* in *Going further*. ::: **1. Baseline.** See the starter file at work before you change it. **Prompt (Claude Code):** ```text Read data/raw/voles_metabolism.csv and make a quick exploratory plot of mass_post_g by treatment arm. Show the R code in your reply; do not create any files. ``` Look for the canaryA fixed line that an instruction file asks the assistant to include in its output, so that seeing the line shows the file was loaded. It does not show that the other rules were followed., `# agents-md: active v1`, as the first line of the code: it shows `AGENTS.md` was loaded. **Answer each request with plain Yes or No.** Never choose an option that says *don't ask again*: it saves a rule that skips the question from then on. Here, answer No if it asks to create or run anything: you asked only to see the code. :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## The starter `AGENTS.md` The canary is a fixed first line that the file asks the assistant to put in any R code it writes. When you see it, you know the file was loaded. Asking for the code in the reply gives the canary somewhere to appear. The "Tests" rules ask the agent to prove its own work after every edit; later blocks rely on this. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` markdown # Project conventions: voles analysis ## Canary When you write or edit R code, make the first line of the first code block: # agents-md: active v1 ## Structure - Raw data live in data/raw/ and are never modified. - Derived data go to data/derived/; figures and tables go to outputs/. - Reusable functions live in scripts/functions/. ## R style - Tidyverse style, native pipe |>, snake_case names, <- for assignment. - Write TRUE and FALSE, never T and F. - Build every path with here::here() (or here() after library(here)). Never use setwd() or rm(list = ls()). - Read CSV files with readr and explicit col_types. ## Reproducibility - Packages are managed with renv. Do not call install.packages(); ask before adding a package. - Do not edit renv.lock. - Set a seed immediately before any random step. - Every script must run in a fresh R session. - Before you report a task done, run each new script once with Rscript from the project root and report the exit status. - Save figures with ggsave() to outputs/. ## Tests - Before you report a task done, run Rscript -e "testthat::test_dir('tests')" once and paste the final summary line verbatim. - Never edit anything in tests/fixtures/, an existing expectation or a tolerance to make a test pass. - Every new function in scripts/functions/ gets a test with at least one known-answer case on a small tibble, including an NA; expected values are worked out by hand, never by running the code under test. ## Data integrity - Never drop rows silently; state the reason for every filter in a comment. - Report the number of observations behind every summary statistic. ## Statistics - Label each analysis as exploratory or confirmatory. - Never type numerical results into text; compute them in code. ## Version control - Before you edit any file, run git status. - If this folder is not a git repository, stop and ask me to set one up. - If there are uncommitted changes, list them and ask whether I want to commit first. - Never commit, push or change git settings unless I ask. ## Working with me - Before changing more than one file, present a plan and wait for approval. - Do not edit anything under data/raw/, tests/fixtures/ or .github/. The one exception: a skill may run tests/make_reference.R once, to capture a reference that does not exist yet. ``` ::: ::: ::: **2. Make it yours.** Open `AGENTS.md` from the Files pane (or run `usethis::edit_file("AGENTS.md")`), and: 1. delete one rule you do not actually follow, from *Structure*, *R style*, *Reproducibility* or *Data integrity*; 2. add one convention you always follow, on one line and specific enough to check ("use the native pipe `|>`", not "write clean code"). Keep the canary and the *Tests*, *Statistics*, *Version control* and *Working with me* sections: later blocks and `tests/test_controls.R` rely on them. Save the file. :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## What makes an instruction work Use `AGENTS.md` for what is always true: structure, style, reproducibility rules. Instructions that work are: - **One per line**, and specific enough to check ("use the native pipe `|>`", not "write clean code"). - **True of your own code**, or the model gets mixed signals. - **Short**, because the file loads into every request. - **Added when a mistake repeats:** a correction in chat is forgotten in the next conversation. - **Not a guarantee:** "never edit raw data" belongs here *and* in the enforced controls of [Block 5](11f-enforced-controls.qmd). ::: **3. Verify.** Type `/memory` and check that `AGENTS.md` is listed. Press Esc rather than choosing it: choosing it opens the file in an external editor. Type `/clear`, then repeat the step 1 prompt. The canary shows the file was **loaded**. To see whether it was **followed**, check the plot code against your new rule. **4. Check it with a test.** Restart R (*Session → Restart R*). Then run this in the R console: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} testthat::test_dir(here::here("tests")) ``` ::: Then commit `AGENTS.md` from the Git pane. **You are done when** the canary appears, the test suite has no failures (tests for later blocks skip), and your edited `AGENTS.md` is committed. **If it goes wrong:** if `/memory` does not list `AGENTS.md`, delete any `CLAUDE.md` you created (*How it works*, below). Also check that `claude --version` is 2.1.281 or later ([setup](11a-setup-claude-code.qmd)). If `test_controls.R` fails, restore the canary or the `git status` line. A failure in `test_explore.R` or `test_ai_log.R` is left over from Block 3. Still stuck? Compare with the `checkpoint-skills` branch. :::: ::: :::::::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## How it works: which files Claude Code reads :::::: {.dia .dia-lanes role="figure" aria-label="Which files Claude Code reads: AGENTS.md, at the start of every conversation; a skill, kept in .agents/skills/your-skill and copied to .claude/skills/your-skill, which Claude Code reads"} ::::: {.dia-flow} ::: {.dia-label} Instruction file: loaded into every conversation ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-file} `AGENTS.md`: your conventions ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} read by ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-ai} Claude Code ::: ::::: ::::: {.dia-flow} ::: {.dia-label} Skills: loaded when invoked or judged relevant ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-file} `.agents/skills//` (the master copy) ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} you copy ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-file} `.claude/skills//` ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} read by ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-ai} Claude Code ::: ::::: ::: {.dia-caption} The course's own skills already ship in both folders; Activity 2 shows how to copy one you write. ::: :::::: Claude Code reads `AGENTS.md`, at the repository root, at the start of every conversation. It does so because the template ships no `CLAUDE.md`. Creating one (for example with `/init`) would hide your conventions. `/memory` lists the instruction files that Claude Code loaded. Choosing one opens it in an external editor, which may be vi on macOS, so edit `AGENTS.md` from the Files pane instead. ::::::: ## Activity 2: Install a skill and test it A skill is a folder that holds a `SKILL.md` file. The file starts with front matterThe block between two lines of three dashes at the top of a file, holding settings such as a skill’s name and description, or a Quarto document’s options. between two lines of three dashes. The front matter gives a `name` and a `description`, and **the description is the trigger**. A skill described as "Use when producing a ggplot2 figure for a report, poster or paper" loads when it should; one described as "for plots" loads unpredictably. The body is the procedure. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} A house figure style (15 minutes) :::: ::::{.task-container} **Goal:** install a skill and grade a figure made with it against your instructor's baseline made without it, so that you judge the skill by what it changes, not by its own report. **Start state:** your workshop repository on `main`, Git pane clean (your `AGENTS.md` committed), Claude Code running in Manual mode in the Terminal tab. **1. The baseline, made without the skill.** Your instructor runs this prompt on screen, before the skill exists. You do not run it. **Instructor:** post the figure in the Zoom chat; learners grade against it in step 4. **Prompt (Claude Code, run by your instructor):** ```text Make a figure of mass_post_g by treatment_arm for the voles data, for a lab report. Save the code as scripts/fig_baseline.R. ``` **2. Create the skill.** In the R console, run `usethis::edit_file(".agents/skills/house-figures/SKILL.md")`. It creates and opens the file. Open the box below and copy the skill into the file, then save it. As you copy, read its `description` and six rules: step 4 grades three of them. :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## The `house-figures` skill: copy this into `SKILL.md` ```markdown --- name: house-figures description: >- Applies this project's conventions to any ggplot2 figure that will appear in a report, poster or paper. Use when asked to create, revise or polish a figure for presentation. Not for quick exploratory plots. --- # House figure style ## Rules 1. Where any group has fewer than 30 observations, show every observation (jittered points or a dot plot) with a summary overlaid. Never draw a bar with error bars ("dynamite plot"). 2. Colour categorical groups with the Okabe-Ito palette (grDevices::palette.colors(palette = "Okabe-Ito")), and map the same variable to point shape so the figure works without colour. 3. Axis titles give the quantity and its unit, for example "Body mass (g)". 4. Use theme_classic(base_size = 12). 5. Show the number of observations per group on the figure. 6. Never add p-values or significance markers unless the user supplies a fitted model and asks for them. ## Before returning code List which rules you applied, and any you could not apply and why. ``` ::: Copy it into `.claude/skills/`, where Claude Code reads it: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} fs::dir_copy( here::here(".agents", "skills", "house-figures"), here::here(".claude", "skills", "house-figures"), overwrite = TRUE ) ``` ::: Type `/skills`: `house-figures` should be listed. :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## How it works: two skill folders `.agents/skills/` holds the master copy. Other tools, such as Posit Assistant, read it directly. Claude Code reads `.claude/skills/`, so copy the folder again whenever you change the skill. The deny rules keep the agent's edit tools out of `.claude/`, so you make the copy yourself. They do not cover `.agents/skills/`, so check the master copy in the Git pane too. On macOS or Linux you can link the folders instead of copying them: see *Going further*. A skill suits a procedure, such as producing a publication figure or cleaning data against a codebook. It can hold scripts or templates beside `SKILL.md`. Its body sets out the procedure: when to use it, the steps, hard rules and a final check. The body loads only when the skill is used, so it can be longer than `AGENTS.md`. Invoking a skill by name (`/skill-name`) always works. Claude Code picks up a new skill in `.claude/skills/` without a restart. If `/skills` does not list it, type `/reload-skills`. For a skill that writes files, `disable-model-invocation: true` in the front matter makes it run only when you invoke it by name. ::: **3. With the skill.** **Prompt (Claude Code):** ```text /house-figures Make a figure of mass_post_g by treatment_arm for the voles data, for a lab report. Save the code as scripts/fig_house.R. ``` It may ask to run `git status` before it edits, because `AGENTS.md` asks it to check. That command only reads, so Yes is fine. Read the edit before you approve it. Approve a run only if you can say what it does and why you want it now; refusing is always safe. So if it asks to run the new script, choose **No**: you run it yourself next. **4. Grade it.** Restart R (*Session → Restart R*). Run `source(here::here("scripts", "fig_house.R"))`, then open the figure it saved in `outputs/`. Compare it with your instructor's baseline on three rules you can see at a glance: | Rule | Baseline (no skill) | Your figure (with skill) | |---|---|---| | 1. Raw data shown; no dynamite plot | | | | 2. Okabe-Ito colour plus shape | | | | 5. n per group shown | | | **5. Record it.** Add a line to `docs/ai-log.md`, as in Block 3. Name the skill and say what you kept or changed in its output. Commit the log with the skill (both folders) and `scripts/fig_house.R`. **You are done when** the table is filled in from the figures you looked at, not from the agent's list of rules it applied, and your log line is committed. **If it goes wrong:** if `/skills` does not list it, check that `.claude/skills/house-figures/SKILL.md` exists, and that its front matter starts and ends with three dashes. If no figure appears in `outputs/`, ask the agent to save it there with `ggsave()`, as `AGENTS.md` asks. Out of time? First commit or discard your changes in the Git pane, so that nothing blocks the switch. Then switch to `checkpoint-skills`. :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Stretch: test the trigger Start a new conversation (`/clear`) and test the trigger. "Give me a quick look at mass_post_g by arm" should *not* load the skill. "Make a figure of metabolic_rate_post by treatment_arm for a poster" should. Or test rule 6: ask it to "add significance stars between the groups in scripts/fig_house.R" and see whether it declines. Either way, the grading in step 4 is what makes the output trustworthy, and you can repeat it on every figure. **Payoff.** What did the skill do for you, how long did checking it take, and would you use it for the next figure? ::: :::: ::: :::{.callout-note} ## Check · Reproduce · Record - **You can now:** state your conventions once, and package a procedure as a skill, **trusted because** the canary and `tests/test_controls.R` show the files are connected, and you grade the output rule by rule. - **Check:** a canary shows a file was loaded, not followed. - **Reproduce:** your `AGENTS.md` states the reproducibility rules; Blocks 7 and 8 check the agent kept to them. - **Record:** your log line from step 5. ::: ## Check your understanding **Your canary line does not appear in Claude Code's answers. What is the most likely explanation?**
**What is the main difference between an instruction file and a skill?**
**A skill fires for quick exploratory plots when you meant it only for publication figures. What should you change first?**
## Going further (not covered live) This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if it is useful to you. :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Skills you did not write Claude Code ships built-in skills such as `/code-review` and `/debug`. Shared collections are also published online, for example Anthropic's `anthropics/skills` repository. Read any skill before you install it: it can include scripts that the assistant runs on your machine. *Install a skill bundle and compare*, below, gives you one to practise on: `pub-figures`, which packages the ggplot chapter's conventions as a skill. ::: :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Linking a skill instead of copying it On macOS or Linux you can use a symbolic linkA file-system entry that points to another folder or file, so one copy can appear in two places. On Windows, copying the folder is usually simpler. instead of a copy, so there is only one version to keep up to date. First delete the copy with `fs::dir_delete(here::here(".claude", "skills", "house-figures"))`. Then create the link with `fs::link_create(here::here(".agents", "skills", "house-figures"), here::here(".claude", "skills", "house-figures"))`. Claude Code follows the link. The link stores the full path, so recreate it if you move the project. On Windows, symbolic links need extra configuration, so copy the folder. ::: :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Instruction and skill files in other tools | File or folder | Posit Assistant | GitHub Copilot | |---|---|---| | `AGENTS.md` (repository root) | Read as project memory | Read by the cloud agent, agent mode and the CLI | | `CLAUDE.md` | — | Read by the cloud agent | | `.github/copilot-instructions.md` | Offered for conversion by `/import-instructions` | Read by Copilot | | Path-scoped rules | No equivalent found | `.github/instructions/*.instructions.md` with `applyTo` | | `.agents/skills//` | Yes | Yes | | `.claude/skills//` | — | Yes | | `.github/skills//` | — | Yes | This course has no `CLAUDE.md`, so every tool reads the same `AGENTS.md`. Copilot reads both `.agents/skills/` and `.claude/skills/`; if it lists a skill twice, remove one route for Copilot. Posit Assistant also includes built-in skills such as `quarto-authoring` and `r-package-development`. ::: :::::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## A rule for Quarto files only Some rules are right for one kind of file and wrong elsewhere. A chunk option such as `#| echo: false` is meaningful in a `.qmd` file and meaningless in an `.R` script. The test for a scoped rule: would it be *wrong*, not merely irrelevant, in the files it excludes? If not, put it in `AGENTS.md`. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Create and test a scoped rule :::: ::::{.task-container} **Goal:** make a rule that loads only for Quarto files and check that it does, so that a convention that is wrong elsewhere stays out of your R scripts. The rules themselves: ```markdown # Quarto document conventions - Set chunk options with the hashpipe (#|) inside the chunk, not in the {r} header. - Give every chunk a label; prefix figure chunks with fig-. - Every figure chunk sets #| fig-cap:, #| fig-width: and #| fig-height:. - Refer to figures in the text with @fig-..., never by a typed number. - Default to #| echo: false unless the document is a code walkthrough. - Resolve paths with here::here(); never assume the working directory is the document's folder. ``` (The "hashpipe" is the `#|` at the start of a chunk-option line.) Put the rules where your tool looks for them: - **Claude Code:** `.claude/rules/quarto.md`. Create it yourself, for example with `usethis::edit_file(".claude/rules/quarto.md")`, because the deny rules keep the agent out of `.claude/`. Begin the file with front matter that restricts it to Quarto files: ```text --- paths: - "**/*.qmd" --- ``` - **Copilot:** `.github/instructions/quarto.instructions.md`, beginning with this front matter: ```text --- applyTo: "**/*.qmd" --- ``` - **Posit Assistant:** no path-scoped instruction file is documented. Add the rules to `AGENTS.md` under a heading such as "When editing .qmd files", or rely on its built-in `quarto-authoring` skill. **Test.** Open a `.qmd` file, then ask for a chunk that plots `mass_post_g` by `treatment_arm`. A correct answer uses hashpipe options, a `fig-` label, a caption and `here::here()`. Then ask for the same plot in an `.R` script; the Quarto rules should not appear. If they do not appear in the `.qmd` either, the rule is not loading in your tool. Report what you found; behaviour differs between tools. **You are done when** you know whether the rules appeared for the `.qmd` chunk and stayed out of the `.R` script on your tool. :::: ::: Every scoped rule is a second copy of a convention to keep in step, once per tool. Use scoped rules sparingly. ::::: :::::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Install a skill bundle and compare `house-figures` is six rules that you wrote and can read at a glance. `pub-figures` is the opposite case. It packages the conventions from the ggplot chapter as a skill of about 200 lines, with R scripts that the assistant sources and adapts. Those conventions are the chart-type and audience tables, `theme_project()`, colorspace palettes, the colour-vision-deficiency check, the four-element legend and saving in two formats. You did not write this skill, so you read it before you install it. The bundle contains: ```text pub-figures/ ├── SKILL.md when to use it, the rules, a pre-flight checklist ├── theme-project.R theme_project() and palette functions ├── raincloud-template.R figure skeleton, including saving ├── emmeans-bridge.R model-based significance brackets └── patchwork-template.R multi-panel figure with one shared legend ``` In the ggplot chapter you wrote a simple `theme_project()`. The `theme_project()` in this bundle is the full version. It keeps the same name and `base_size` argument, and adds a font, colours for titles and gridlines, and an `axis_type` argument. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} A skill bundle you did not write :::: ::::{.task-container} **Goal:** install a skill you did not write, run it by name and check its output yourself, so that you know what it does before you rely on it. **1. Read before you install.** Open `SKILL.md` and `theme-project.R` (both are also reproduced below). Find two places where `pub-figures` contradicts your `house-figures` rules. (There are at least two: the palette and the theme.) Find the line that tells the assistant what to do when information is missing. **2. Install.** In the R console, run `unzip(file.choose(), exdir = here::here(".agents", "skills"))`. It lets you pick the downloaded zip and unpacks it into `.agents/skills/`. Then copy the skill into `.claude/skills/` for Claude Code: use the `fs::dir_copy()` line above, changing `house-figures` to `pub-figures`. The skill uses ggdist, colorspace, ragg, colorBlindness, emmeans and ggpubr. If your project uses renv and they are not in its lockfileThe renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment., add them yourself before the test. Do not let the assistant install packages. **3. Same prompt, named skill.** Both skills describe themselves as being for figures in reports, posters and papers, so a plain request could load either. Overlapping descriptions are a real hazard once you collect skills from several sources. So name the one you want. Type `/skills` to check that it is listed (skills reload without a restart). Then run this prompt: **Prompt (Claude Code):** ```text /pub-figures Make a figure of mass_post_g by treatment_arm for the voles data, for a lab report. ``` Did the assistant ask about the audience, or record a default? **4. Grade it against its own checklist.** The skill ends with a pre-flight checklist. Check the script against each item yourself; do not accept the assistant's report that it did. Then run the script: are both a PDF and a PNG in `outputs/figures/`? Run the `colorBlindness::cvdPlot()` line it left for you, then look at the result. **5. Test a rule under pressure.** Ask it to "add significance stars between the groups" without fitting a model. The skill says it must insert a legend placeholder rather than invent p-values. Then give it a fitted model it can actually see. Claude Code cannot see objects in your R console, so a model you fit there does not count. Ask it to add `model <- lm(mass_post_g ~ treatment_arm, data = voles)` to the figure script itself, or paste the output of `summary(model)` into the prompt. Then ask for the stars again: it should now use the `emmeans-bridge.R` pattern with an adjusted p-value. **6. Compare.** Which skill would you hand to a colleague? Which would you trust without rereading it after an update? A long skill encodes more of your standards, and hides more of them from view. **You are done when** you have checked the figure script against the skill's pre-flight checklist yourself, seen how it handles significance stars without and with a model, and decided which skill you would hand to a colleague. :::: ::: :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## `pub-figures/SKILL.md` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ```` markdown --- name: pub-figures description: >- Use when producing a ggplot2 figure intended for sharing outside the immediate session, including manuscript figures, lab reports, posters, talk slides, and public engagement graphics. Do not invoke for diagnostic, exploratory, model-checking, or one-off plots. --- # Publication figures This skill governs production of figures that will be seen by an external audience. It is self-contained: the house rules below apply even if the project has no instruction file. ## House rules - Tidyverse style, native pipe `|>`, `here::here()` for every path. - British spelling in titles, labels, legends and comments. - Never produce pie charts, dual y-axes, 3D effects, or bar charts with error bars ("dynamite plots") when the raw data exist. ## Missing information If information you need is missing (the audience, a variable's unit, the fitted model), ask the user once, in a single message, before writing code. If the user tells you to proceed without it, or you are working unattended (for example as a cloud agent on a pull request), choose the safe default this skill gives, record the choice in a code comment and, if there is one, in the pull request description, and continue. ## Project toolkit The packages this skill uses are listed below. Check that each one you need is in `renv.lock`; if one is missing, stop and ask before installing anything: - `ggplot2`, `patchwork`, `here`, `scales` for core plotting, composition, paths, and label formatting. - `ggdist` for raincloud and half-eye distributions: `stat_halfeye()`, `stat_pointinterval()`. - `ggbeeswarm` for moderate-n group displays: `geom_quasirandom()`. - `colorspace` for palettes: `scale_*_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark 2")`, `scale_*_continuous_sequential(palette = "Viridis")`, `scale_*_continuous_diverging(palette = "Blue-Red")`, and the HCL generators (`sequential_hcl()`, `diverging_hcl()`) used by the brand-seeded scales in `theme-project.R`. - `emmeans` for estimated marginal means and pairwise contrasts: `emmeans(model, specs = "var")`, `pairs(emm, adjust = "tukey")`. - `ggpubr::stat_pvalue_manual()` as the rendering layer for emmeans-derived contrasts. Never `ggpubr::stat_compare_means()`, which performs unadjusted pairwise t-tests by default. - `ggh4x` for nested or hierarchical faceting: `facet_nested()`, `facet_nested_wrap()`, `guide_axis_nested()`. - `ragg` for raster output via `ggsave(device = ragg::agg_png)`. - `colorBlindness::cvdPlot()` for the colour-vision-deficiency check. - `showtext` (optional) for the project font; without it `theme_project()` falls back to the device's default font. Do not introduce additional plotting packages without amending this list. Do not reach for `cowplot` themes when `theme_minimal()` or `theme_project()` will do. Do not hand-write manual hex colour vectors as data scales: use the `colorspace` palettes or the brand-seeded constructors in `theme-project.R`, both of which keep palettes CVD-checkable. A single fixed colour for a single-group or highlight geom is permitted and is not a "data scale". ## Using the files in this skill Source the theme and palette functions from the skill folder: ```r source(here::here(".agents", "skills", "pub-figures", "theme-project.R")) ``` If the folder was copied into `.claude/skills/` rather than linked, use that path instead. `theme_project()` here is the full version of the simple `theme_project()` from the ggplot chapter: same name and `base_size` argument, plus a font, furniture colours and an `axis_type` argument. ## Audience must be determined first Identify the audience as one of `journal-lab-report`, `poster`, `talk`, or `public-engagement` before writing any plotting code. Styling, annotation density, and title framing all depend on the answer. If the audience is not specified, ask (see *Missing information*). If proceeding without an answer, default to `journal-lab-report` and record the assumption at the top of the script: ```r # Audience not specified; defaulting to journal-lab-report. # Re-run with explicit audience if poster, talk, or public-engagement intended. ``` Then state in one sentence each: the variables and their types (continuous, discrete, date/time), the scientific question, the chart type the variable structure calls for, whether raw data will be shown, and whether statistical annotations are required. ## Statistical annotations require a model object Do not annotate test statistics, p-values, or confidence intervals unless a fitted model object exists: fitted by code in this project that you have run or can read, or present in the user's live R session where your tool can see it. Fabricating values from descriptive data is a serious error. If there is no model, omit annotations and insert this placeholder for the legend: > LEGEND PLACEHOLDER. Model object required to supply the test statistic, degrees of freedom, p-value, and adjustment method. Do not fabricate. ## Chart selection | Variable 1 | Variable 2 | Variable 3 | Default chart | |------------|------------|------------|---------------| | Continuous | — | — | Raincloud (`ggdist::stat_halfeye` + boxplot + jitter) | | Continuous | Continuous | — | Scatter plot | | Continuous | Continuous | Discrete | Scatter, colour and shape mapped to discrete | | Discrete | — | — | Bar chart of counts | | Discrete | Continuous | — | Raincloud per group; boxplot if many groups; bar only if one summary value per group | | Discrete | Discrete | — | Heatmap of counts | | Discrete | Discrete | Continuous | Heatmap of the continuous variable | | Date | Continuous | — | Line chart | | Date | Continuous | Discrete | Line chart, one line per group | If a chart not in this table is requested, select the closest matching entry, generate the code, and record both the request and the substitution in a comment at the top of the script (and in the pull request description, if there is one). ## Colour The colour-vision-deficiency check (`cvdPlot()`, below) is the final arbiter: a palette that fails it must be replaced, regardless of brand intent. **No brand specified (default).** Use `colorspace::scale_*` functions, matched to data structure. **Brand specified.** When the request names a brand colour (for example, "use a brand colour of darkblue"), call `set_brand("darkblue")` once after sourcing `theme-project.R`. `set_brand()` accepts any R colour name or hex string. The brand colour then seeds: - single-colour and highlight geoms, via `brand_base()`; - sequential continuous scales: `scale_*_brand_seq()`; - the **high** arm of diverging continuous scales: `scale_*_brand_div(midpoint = )`. The low arm is the brand's complementary hue, so the two arms always contrast, unless you name a second brand colour with `set_brand(, div_low = )`. **Categorical colour is never brand-seeded.** One seed colour cannot generate a coherent, CVD-safe set of distinct hues. For unordered groups, use `colorspace` "Dark 2"; `scale_*_brand_qual()` in `theme-project.R` is the same palette and takes no `base` or `n` argument. The brand colour can still mark one focal group, with the other groups in grey. | Data structure | Palette type | colorspace default | With a brand set | |----------------|--------------|--------------------|------------------| | Discrete, unordered groups | Qualitative | `Dark 2` | `Dark 2` (`scale_*_brand_qual()` is identical) | | Discrete, ordered groups | Sequential discrete | `Purples 3` | `Purples 3` (the brand scales are continuous only) | | Continuous, one-directional | Sequential | `Viridis` | `scale_*_brand_seq()` | | Continuous, midpoint-centred | Diverging | `Blue-Red` | `scale_*_brand_div()` | If a brand-seeded scale fails the CVD check, replace it with the colorspace default in the same row and record the fallback in a comment. Categorical groupings must use redundant encoding: shape for points, linetype for lines. Colour alone is not sufficient. ## Audience-specific styling | Element | Journal / lab report | Poster | Talk | Public engagement | |---------|---------------------|--------|------|-------------------| | Title above figure | No | Yes (explanatory) | Yes (explanatory) | Yes (explanatory) | | Figure legend below | Yes (four elements) | Optional, abbreviated | No | No | | Direct labelling | Sparingly | Yes | Yes | Yes | | Highlighting (grey out non-focal) | No | Yes | Yes | Yes | | Reference lines | Sparingly | Yes | Yes | Yes | | Statistical annotations | Precise p-values | Abbreviated | One key result | None | | Base font size | 12 pt floor | 16 to 20 pt | 14 to 18 pt | 14 to 18 pt | | Raw data shown | Always where n permits | Always | Always | Where it clarifies | `theme_project()` defaults to `base_size = 12`, the journal/lab-report floor. Raise it explicitly via `theme_project(base_size = ...)` for poster, talk, and public-engagement figures per this table. Descriptive titles state what the figure shows. Explanatory titles state what it means. Journal figures put descriptive framing in the legend, not the title. ## Showing raw data | n per group | Display | |-------------|---------| | Up to ~30 | Strip plot or raincloud, all points visible | | ~30 to ~300 | Raincloud with jittered points, alpha 0.3 to 0.5 | | ~300 to ~3000 | Beeswarm or 2D density | | > ~3000 | Hexbin or 2D contour | ## Statistical annotations workflow Pairwise contrasts come from `emmeans::emmeans()` and `emmeans::pairs()` with an explicit adjustment method (`tukey`, `holm`, or similar). Render brackets with `ggpubr::stat_pvalue_manual()`, supplying a data frame of contrasts. Filter to significant contrasts before drawing. Format p-values with `scales::label_pvalue()` so very small values appear as `<0.001` rather than `0.000`. A worked example is in `emmeans-bridge.R`. ## Error bars Three options, not interchangeable: - **Standard deviation:** spread of individual observations. Use when describing population variability. - **Standard error of the mean:** precision of the sample mean. Shrinks with sample size. - **95% confidence interval:** the recommended default. Prefer model-based intervals via `emmeans` where a model exists, otherwise from `stat_summary(fun.data = mean_cl_normal)`. The choice must appear in the y axis label. ## Multiple panels and shared legends When composing panels with `patchwork` and `plot_layout(guides = "collect")`, collection merges only guides that are identical in aesthetic, scale, breaks, and title (`name`). It deduplicates by guide specification, not by visual appearance, and it never removes a guide it judges different. Two failures follow: panels that encode the same variable through different aesthetics (`fill` in one, `colour` plus `shape` in another) or different palettes produce one legend each; and a panel encoding a genuinely different variable produces its own legend, which is correct. Resolve the layout from the plot specifications: - **Same variable, same palette, across all panels:** produce one shared legend. Designate the panel with the richest encoding (e.g. colour plus shape) as the legend-bearer, because that legend is a complete key for the simpler panels but not the reverse. Apply the identical scale call and an identical `name` in every panel, then suppress the guide on every non-bearing panel with `guides( = "none")`. Record the choice of bearer in a comment. - **Panels encode different variables:** do not force collection into one key. Keep the separate legends; merging them would mislabel a panel. A mismatched `name`, a differing aesthetic or scale, or a missing suppression line will silently leave more than one legend for the same variable. After composing, confirm exactly one legend appears per distinct variable. A worked skeleton is in `patchwork-template.R`. ## Saving Always save to `outputs/figures/` via `here::here()` in both PDF and PNG formats. Specify `width`, `height`, `units`, and `dpi` explicitly; do not rely on `ggsave()` defaults. Use `ragg::agg_png` as the device for PNG output with `bg = "white"`. PDF uses the default device. ## Accessibility check The agent cannot verify visual accessibility. Insert this line at the end of the script and flag it for the investigator to run and inspect: ```r if (interactive()) colorBlindness::cvdPlot(fig1) ``` If the four-panel simulation shows groups becoming indistinguishable under deuteranopia, protanopia, or tritanopia, the palette or redundant encoding must be revised. For brand-seeded scales, a failed check requires falling back to the `colorspace` default named in the colour table; brand intent does not override accessibility. ## Pre-flight checklist (agent-verifiable items only) Before declaring the script complete, confirm: - Both axes labelled with name and unit, or just name for dimensionless variables. - Bar chart axes start at zero; other axes cropped to the data range. - Faceted panels share scale unless a comment justifies freeing it. - Composite figures collect to one legend per distinct variable; non-bearing panels suppress their guide with `guides(... = "none")` and all retained scales share an identical `name`. - Palette applied via `colorspace::scale_*` functions or the brand-seeded constructors in `theme-project.R`, never hand-written hex vectors as data scales. Single fixed colours for single-group or highlight geoms are permitted. - Categorical colour uses `Dark 2` (directly or via `scale_*_brand_qual()`), not a brand-seeded palette. - A brand-seeded scale that the colour-vision-deficiency check would fail is replaced by its `colorspace` default; the fallback is recorded in a comment. - Categorical grouping carries redundant encoding (shape or linetype). - Statistical annotations sourced from a fitted model object, never from descriptive data. - None of the forbidden chart types in *House rules*. - Default theme is `theme_project()`, `theme_minimal()`, or `theme_classic()`. Never `theme_grey()`. - `theme_project()` base font size matches the audience floor (12 pt journal; 14 to 20 pt otherwise). - File saved to `outputs/figures/` as both PDF and PNG with explicit dimensions. - `cvdPlot()` call, wrapped in `if (interactive())`, inserted at the end of the script with a comment flagging it for the investigator. ## Supplementary files in this skill directory - `raincloud-template.R`: figure skeleton with palette, theme, and saving. - `emmeans-bridge.R`: worked emmeans-to-ggpubr annotation pattern. - `theme-project.R`: project theme plus brand-seeded HCL palette constructors. - `patchwork-template.R`: composite-figure skeleton with collected legend and guide suppression. ```` ::: ::: ::: :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## `pub-figures/theme-project.R` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # ============================================================================== # Project theme and palette construction for ggplot2. # # Colour policy (authoritative; see pub-figures SKILL.md): # * No brand set -> use colorspace palettes directly. # * Brand set -> set_brand("darkblue") sets the base colour (used by # single-colour and highlight geoms) and reseeds the # sequential ramp and the diverging HIGH arm. Wrapped in # interactive() so a run with Rscript does not write a stray Rplots.pdf. if (interactive()) colorBlindness::cvdPlot(fig1) ``` ::: ::: :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## `pub-figures/emmeans-bridge.R` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # emmeans-bridge.R # Worked emmeans-to-ggpubr annotation pattern. # Requires a fitted model object: fitted by code in this project that you have # run or can read, or present in the user's live R session where your tool can # see it. Never fabricate test statistics from descriptive data. library(emmeans) library(ggpubr) library(dplyr) library(tibble) library(tidyr) library(stringr) library(ggplot2) library(scales) # model <- lm(value ~ group, data = data) # supplied upstream # fig1 <- ggplot(data, aes(group, value)) + geom_boxplot() # supplied upstream # # ADAPT: `fig1` is your existing ggplot. `panel_yrange()` reads layer 1 by # default, which must be the geom whose data the brackets sit above (e.g. the # boxplot). If layer 1 is a reference line or similar, pass the correct index, # e.g. panel_yrange(fig1, layer = 2L). emm <- emmeans::emmeans(model, specs = "group") # lowest and highest y values drawn by one layer ---- panel_yrange <- function(p, layer = 1L) { d <- ggplot2::ggplot_build(p)$data[[layer]] # positional y columns ggplot may compute cols <- intersect( c("ymin_final", "ymin", "lower", "ymax_final", "ymax", "upper", "y"), names(d) ) if (length(cols) == 0L) { stop("No y-position column found in layer ", layer, ".") } range(unlist(d[cols]), na.rm = TRUE) } y_range <- panel_yrange(fig1) # step between brackets as a fraction of the data range, so positions work for # negative values and for data far from zero y_step <- 0.07 * diff(y_range) contrasts_df <- pairs(emm, adjust = "tukey") |> as_tibble() |> separate_wider_delim( contrast, delim = " - ", names = c("group1", "group2") ) |> # emmeans wraps level names containing spaces or operators in parentheses dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across( c(group1, group2), \(x) stringr::str_remove_all(x, "^\\(|\\)$") )) |> dplyr::filter(p.value < 0.05) |> dplyr::mutate( p.label = scales::label_pvalue()(p.value), y.position = y_range[2] + y_step * dplyr::row_number() ) # headroom so the top bracket isn't clipped: highest position + one more step y_top <- y_range[2] + y_step * (nrow(contrasts_df) + 1) fig1 + stat_pvalue_manual( contrasts_df, label = "p.label", tip.length = 0.01 ) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(NA, y_top)) ``` ::: ::: :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## `pub-figures/patchwork-template.R` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # Composite figure: panels sharing ONE collected legend. # # Precondition: every panel maps the SAME grouping variable to the SAME palette. # If a panel encodes a different variable, do not use this pattern for it; give it # its own scale and accept a separate legend (forcing one key would mislabel it). # # Colour policy (see pub-figures SKILL.md): # * The shared grouping variable is categorical, so every panel uses # colorspace qualitative "Dark 2", with or without a brand. Categorical # colour is never brand-seeded. Keep an identical `name` across panels so # the legend collects to one. # # Legend-bearer: chosen here by richness of encoding. If unclear, use the panel # with the most aesthetics mapped to the group and record the choice. # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- library(ggplot2) library(patchwork) # Legend-bearing panel: richest encoding (colour + shape), legend retained. # Redundant encoding (shape) is required by the skill, and conveniently makes this # panel a complete key for the simpler ones. p_keep <- data |> ggplot(aes(x = x1, y = y1, colour = group_var, shape = group_var)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.7) + colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark 2", name = "Group") + scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 17, 15), name = "Group") + labs(x = "X1", y = "Y1") # Other panels: identical palette and identical name, guide suppressed. # Suppression is what collection cannot do for you. Repeat per additional panel. p_other <- data |> ggplot(aes(x = x2, y = y2, colour = group_var)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.7) + colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark 2", name = "Group") + labs(x = "X2", y = "Y2") + guides(colour = "none") # Letters refer to plots in the order added (A = p_keep, B = p_other). layout <- " AB " fig1 <- p_keep + p_other + patchwork::plot_layout(design = layout, guides = "collect") + patchwork::plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") & theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.tag = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12)) fig1 ``` ::: ::: ::::: ## Glossary ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
term definition
canary A fixed line that an instruction file asks the assistant to include in its output, so that seeing the line shows the file was loaded. It does not show that the other rules were followed.
front matter The block between two lines of three dashes at the top of a file, holding settings such as a skill's name and description, or a Quarto document's options.
instruction file A file the assistant loads into every conversation, such as AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, stating the project's standing conventions. Its contents are requests, not guarantees.
lockfile The renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment.
skill A folder containing a SKILL.md file (and optionally scripts and templates) that an assistant loads only when it is invoked by name or judged relevant from its description.
symbolic link A file-system entry that points to another folder or file, so one copy can appear in two places. On Windows, copying the folder is usually simpler.
